title: Beyond the Screen: IFFI 2026 Brings India's Cinematic Legacy to the Printed Page
subtitle: Two publications released by Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, spotlight cinematic thought, creative journeys and the unfinished legacy of filmmaker Awtar Kaul
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
Cinema captures the imagination of generations, reflecting society, preserving memories and shaping cultural identities. Beyond the moving images on screen, books play an equally important role in documenting the ideas, creative processes and journeys that shape the cinematic landscape. Recognising this significance, the Publications Division released two books at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026, celebrating different dimensions of India's cinematic heritage.
Speaking on the occasion, Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, emphasised the importance of documenting the creative journeys behind films and preserving India's rich cinematic heritage for posterity. He observed that cinema is not merely a medium of entertainment but also a reflection of society, the spirit of different generations and evolving ideas. “Films tell us a story. Books on cinema help us understand how these stories came to life,” he said, highlighting how publications offer valuable insights into the experiences of filmmakers, the evolution of cinematic techniques and the ideas that have shaped Indian cinema.
The two books released on the occasion were
Cinema: Vividh Aayam
, compiled by Shri Rajendra Bhatt, and
Awtar Kaul: The (In)Complete Story
, authored by Shri Vinod Kaul. While the former brings together important writings and perspectives on cinema, making them accessible to Hindi readers, the latter documents the life and unfinished creative legacy of filmmaker Awtar Kaul.
Referring to
Cinema: Vividh Aayam
, Shri Chanchal Kumar appreciated the collection of writings by filmmakers and scholars, offering insights into celebrated films, filmmaking and world cinema. He particularly appreciated the effort to make these works accessible to Hindi readers. Speaking about
Awtar Kaul: The (In)Complete Story
, he recalled the legacy of filmmaker Awtar Kaul, whose only film,
27 Down
(1974), became a landmark of Indian New Wave cinema.
Congratulating the Publications Division, Shri Rajendra Bhatt, Shri Vinod Kaul and all those associated with the publications, the Secretary expressed hope that the books would inspire students, filmmakers and cinema enthusiasts to explore India's cinematic heritage more deeply.
Ms. Kanchan Prasad, Director General, Publications Division, highlighted the Division's longstanding association with cinema and its role in documenting India's cultural and creative heritage. Observing that while cinema captures moments in time, books ensure that these moments are preserved, she spoke about the Division's efforts to document creative journeys, preserve stories and celebrate the contributions of those who have shaped India's cultural identity.
Shri Rajendra Bhatt elaborated on the editorial journey behind
Cinema: Vividh Aayam
, explaining how the Publications Division took forward the initiative of bringing important writings on cinema to Hindi readers.
The session was moderated by Ms. Smita Vats Sharma, Director General, Press Information Bureau, in the presence of Shri Prabhat, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and Dr. K. K. Nirala, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
About the Books
Awtar Kaul: The (In)Complete Story
Authored in English by Shri Vinod Kaul, the book chronicles the life and unfinished legacy of filmmaker Awtar Kaul through letters, photographs, memories and conversations. His only film,
27 Down
(1974), became a milestone of Indian New Wave cinema and won the National Film Award. The award was announced on the very day he tragically drowned in Mumbai at the age of 34 while attempting to save a friend.
Cinema: Vividh Aayam
Compiled in Hindi by Shri Rajendra Bhatt, this anthology brings together adapted articles and dialogues from FTII's magazine
Lensight
. It offers insights into film history, cinematography, world cinema and the creative processes behind filmmaking, bringing diverse perspectives on cinema to a wider Hindi readership.

title: “Why Should I Be Perfect by Someone Else’s Standards?”: Girish Kasaravalli Champions Cultural Authenticity at IFFI 57
subtitle: Society’s Cruel Process of ‘Othering’ Has Always Been at the Heart of My Stories: Girish Kasaravalli Reflects on 50 Years of Parallel Cinema at 57th IFFI
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
Cinema, for Girish Kasaravalli, is not merely the art of telling stories; it is the courage to confront the stories society refuses to see. From caste and social hierarchies to religious hegemony and the marginalisation of vulnerable communities, the process of ‘othering’ has remained a recurring concern throughout his five-decade-long cinematic journey. This philosophy took centre stage at the ‘In Conversation’ session,
‘The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli’
, held today at Kala Academy, Goa, during the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).
Tracing his remarkable cinematic journey from his 1977 debut
Ghatashraddha
to acclaimed films such as
Tabarana Kathe
,
Thaayi Saheba
and
Dweepa
, the celebrated Kannada filmmaker and 14-time National Film Award laureate challenged the conventional divide between commercial and art-house cinema, emphasising that every cinematic expression carries an ideological position. “There is nothing called ‘only entertainment’. Even entertainment is a political form,” he remarked, underscoring that filmmakers inevitably either endorse or challenge dominant social ideologies.
Reflecting on the evolution of New Kannada Cinema, he spoke about the need to develop an indigenous cinematic language rooted in India's social and cultural realities rather than borrowed frameworks. “Style is not imposed on a film; it comes from within the content itself,” he observed. Articulating his storytelling philosophy, he added, “The plot of the story is not important, but the vision of the story is important.” He identified ‘othering’—the marginalisation and exclusion of vulnerable communities—as a recurring concern at the heart of his films.
Rejecting simplistic moral conclusions, Kasaravalli explained that cinema should provoke thought rather than prescribe judgments. Invoking writer U.R. Ananthamurthy's philosophy of ending every answer with a ‘but’, he said, “To say through a film that ‘this is right, this is wrong’ itself is wrong. I don't make easy judgments, because that forces the audience to think.”
The conversation also explored the portrayal of women and their remarkable resilience in his films. Referring to
Dweepa
, he highlighted protagonist Nagi's pragmatic approach to adversity, recalling her words: “Let me make the present pleasant.” He observed that women often demonstrate an extraordinary ability to negotiate changing circumstances and confront life's uncertainties.
Sharing insights into his creative process, Kasaravalli explained his preference for meticulously detailed scripts over storyboards, enabling his collaborators to translate his visual imagination onto the screen. “Cinema is germinated in my mind, but it is executed by others,” he said, underscoring the collaborative nature of filmmaking. He added that cinema is ultimately about imparting an experience, not merely making statements.
Concluding with a passionate appeal for cultural authenticity, he invoked Julio García Espinosa's philosophy of ‘imperfect cinema’, urging Indian filmmakers to remain rooted in their own cultural and visual identities rather than measure themselves against externally imposed standards. “Why should I be ‘perfect’ by someone else's standards? I should be loyal to my own milieu,” he affirmed.
The session offered an illuminating retrospective of a filmmaker whose five-decade-long contribution to Indian cinema continues to challenge conventions, interrogate social hierarchies and explore the complexities of human dignity and conscience. His reflections also served as a reminder that the strength of Indian cinema lies in its ability to find its own voice, rooted in the country's diverse cultural experiences.
The session was moderated by acclaimed film journalist, critic and author Naman Ramachandran.

content:

Indian Panorama 2026 was formally inaugurated today at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Panaji, Goa, with distinguished members of the Feature and Non-Feature Film Juries being felicitated in recognition of their contribution to curating this year's official selection.
The jury members were honoured by Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Shri G. Krishnakumar, Chairperson, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC); and Shri Ashutosh Gowariker, Festival Director.
Declaring Indian Panorama 2026 open, Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, highlighted the remarkable diversity of Indian cinema since its inception. He observed that the celebration of cinema offers a meaningful opportunity to recognise how every region of the country contributes its distinct languages, cultures and stories. Congratulating the jury members for their thoughtful selections, as well as the Government of Goa and the festival team for organising the event, he expressed his wishes for continued global recognition of Indian cinema.
Addressing the gathering, Shri G. Krishnakumar, Chairperson, NFDC, reflected on the legacy of Indian Panorama since its inception in 1978 and its role in celebrating India's cinematic diversity across languages and regions. Referring to this year's IFFI theme,
Stories Without Borders
, he reaffirmed the Ministry's commitment to cinema and expressed gratitude to the Government of Goa and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for their continued support. He also extended a warm welcome to filmmakers and film enthusiasts attending the festival.
In his welcome address, Festival Director Shri Ashutosh Gowariker recalled his early memories of IFFI and reflected on how Indian Panorama has evolved over the decades into an important showcase of India's rich cultural and cinematic diversity. Highlighting the response to this year's selection process, he noted that the festival received 762 feature film entries and 358 non-feature film entries, taking the total to 1,120 submissions across 18 languages. The final selection spans 14 languages, including Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Tulu, Ladakhi, Kashmiri and English, alongside web series.
Aligning his remarks with the 57th edition's theme,
Stories Without Borders
, Shri Gowariker urged filmmakers, technicians and emerging storytellers to continue telling their stories, while encouraging audiences to watch widely and judge wisely.

title: Beyond Languages and Borders: Indian Panorama Celebrates the Diversity of Indian Cinema at 57th IFFI
subtitle: Jury highlights originality, fresh voices and shared emotions across India’s diverse cinematic traditions
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
From the southernmost regions to the Northeast, Indian cinema draws its strength from a remarkable diversity of stories, cultures and creative expressions. Yet, beyond regional identities and cinematic styles, it is the shared human emotions that connect these stories with audiences across the country. Reflecting this diversity, the Indian Panorama 2026 Feature Film Jury, chaired by filmmaker Madhur Bhandarkar, shared his experience of selecting 25 films from 404 entries at a press conference held at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.
Reflecting on the selection process, Madhur Bhandarkar said the jury encountered films spanning several genres and arrived at its decisions collectively. He described the experience as enriching, noting that film festivals offer opportunities to learn and gain new perspectives. Expressing confidence in the final selection, he said the jury was satisfied with the films chosen. He particularly recalled some Marathi, Ladakhi and Malayalam films that left a strong impression on the jury, describing them as mesmerising.
Emphasising the importance of originality and representation, senior columnist and jury member Bharathi Pradhan said the panel looked for films that retained their original ideas while bringing together perspectives from across the country. She expressed satisfaction that the selection had achieved pan-Indian representation. She also noted that the criteria for selecting films in the Mainstream Cinema section differed from those applied to the Indian Panorama Feature Film section.
For actor and jury member Bindu Chandramouli, watching films from different parts of the country was akin to experiencing international cinema. Despite the differences in languages, styles and genres, she observed a common thread of underlying emotions connecting the films. Encouraging audiences to explore cinema beyond their linguistic preferences, she urged Telugu viewers to remain open to films from different languages and appreciate diverse storytelling styles.
Cinematographer and jury member M. S. Prabhu described the experience as a virtual tour of India, reflecting the country’s unity in diversity. As the jury watched films from different regions, connections between their stories and emotions became increasingly evident. He also appreciated the work of new directors, observing that the selection process itself had been a valuable learning experience.
Sharing his response to the selected films, cinematographer and jury member K. S. Sivaraman said the emotions conveyed by some of the stories were so compelling that he could even imagine adapting certain films for South Indian audiences. Jury member Soham P. Shah highlighted the message conveyed by a film as an important consideration in the selection process.
The jury also discussed the selection of the five films in the Mainstream Cinema section, with Bhandarkar noting that the decision was collective and guided by the potential, concepts and ideas presented by the films. The press conference was moderated by  Shri Rajith Chandran.
The selected feature-film package comprises 20 films in the Indian Panorama Feature Film section and five in the Mainstream Cinema section. Dhurandhar, a Hindi film directed by Aditya Dhar, has been selected as the opening feature film of Indian Panorama 2026. The wider Indian Panorama selection also includes 20 non-feature films.
The jury’s reflections underscored the breadth of Indian filmmaking, where distinct regional identities and cinematic styles come together through stories that resonate across audiences. At IFFI, Indian Panorama continues to bring this diversity into focus, offering a platform for contemporary Indian cinema to be experienced and appreciated across languages and cultures.

title: Celebrating a Century of Cinematic Brilliance: IFFI 2026 Honours Seven Stalwarts of Indian Cinema
subtitle: Uttam Kumar, Shakti Samanta, O.P. Nayyar, Suryakant Mandhare, Prem Nazir, Raaj Kumar and Bombay Ravi: IFFI Celebrates Seven Icons of Indian Cinema born in 1926!
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
The year 1926 proved to be an extraordinary for Indian cinema, as seven remarkable personalities were born into diverse families and cultural traditions across the country, each destined to leave an enduring legacy on the silver screen. They are Uttam Kumar, the legendary ‘Mahanayak’ of Bengali cinema; Shakti Samanta, the celebrated filmmaker behind some of Hindi cinema’s most iconic films; O.P. Nayyar, the music maestro whose timeless melodies continue to enthral generations; Padma Shri awardee Suryakant Mandhare, whose memorable portrayals enriched Marathi cinema across rural, historical and mythological narratives; Prem Nazir, Malayalam cinema’s evergreen romantic hero; Raaj Kumar, the actor whose distinctive voice and inimitable mannerisms made him a cult figure in Bollywood; and Ravi (Bombay Ravi), the gifted composer behind enduring musical treasures such as
Chaudhvin Ka Chand
,
Gumrah
,
Waqt
and
Humraaz
.
A hundred years later, the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) is marking their birth anniversaries with five restored films in four languages, namely, Hindi, Bengali, Malayalam and Marathi. These films are some of the most celebrated works of these centenarian artists. All of these films were restored by the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) under the National Film Heritage Mission, which is the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting’s flagship initiative to preserve, conserve, digitize and restore India’s rich film legacy.
Uttam Kumar in
Chowringhee
The 1965 Bengali classic ‘Chowringhee’ brought to the fore one of the great ensemble performances in Bengali cinema. Uttam Kumar, the most celebrated star of Bengali cinema, accepted the role of Satyasundar ‘Sata’ Bose in the film at a time when he was at the height of popularity. Uttam Kumar started his career as an actor in the year 1948, and since then, acted in more than 200 films over three decades, and gifted classics such as ‘Saptapadi’, ‘Harano Sur’, ‘Nayak’, ‘Chiriyakhana’, ‘Amanush’ among many others. He moved Bengali cinema acting from stage mannerism to urban romanticism.
Uttam Kumar
Director Shakti Samanta and Music Director O.P. Nayyar’s
Kashmir Ki Kali
‘Kashmir ki Kali’ took both the maestros to a peak in their respective careers as a director and music director. Shakti Samanta filmed and presented to cinema-lovers Kashmir’s heavenly beauty in full colour, while O.P. Nayyar created musical scores that still moves people.
Shakti Samanta also started his career in 1948 as an assistant director and debuting with the 1955 film ‘Bahu’. Under his banner of Shakti Films, he directed 43 features, of which 37 are in Hindi, while 6 are in Bengali. The master film maker gifted hindi cinema classics like ‘Howrah Bridge’, ‘China Town’, ‘An Evening in Paris’, ‘Aradhana’. ‘Kati Patang’, ‘Amar Prem’ and ‘Anuraag’.
Omkar Prasad Nayyar started his career in films with ‘Aasmaan’ (1952), and went on to deliver music for ‘Aar Paar’, Mr. & Mrs 55, CID, Naya Daur, and Howrah Bridge. His collaborations with singers Md. Rafi, Asha Bhosle and Geeta Dutt produced some of the all-time favorites of Hindi film music. His horse-trot rhythms and dholak beats created a distinguished pattern of music that audiences admired much.
Shakti Samanta
O.P.Nayyar
Suryakant Mandhare in
Sadhi Manase
Suryakant Madhare was discovered as a boy by his mentor Bhalji Pendharkar and started his career as a child-artist. In a career spanning fifty years, and in over a hundred film, including Sangtye Aika, Kanyadaan, Mohityanchi Manjula and Malhari Martand, he gifted some of Marathi cinema’s strongest characters, ranging from rural, historical to mythological heroes.
In the 1965 classic
Sadhi Manase
, he plays Shankar, the blacksmith, who symbolizes a strong man without swagger, the dignity of work and the ache of being misjudged, opposite Jayshree Gadkar, with whom he has paired in many films. Another interesting fact about the film is that the legendary Lata Mangeshkar composed its music under the pseudonym ‘Anandghan’, which she often used for her work in Marathi cinema.
Suryakant Mandhare
Prem Nazir in
Thulabharam
Malayalam cinema’s evergreen romantic hero Prem Nazir, whose movies are marked for their songs and sunlit live stories, played the role of a factory worker and trade union man Rama in
Thulabharam.
Best known for his romantic hero roles, the iconic actor shed his glamorous screen persona to deliver a remarkably understated performance, arguably one of the finest of his career.
From Irrutinte Atmavu, Murappennu and Nadhi to Kallichellamma, Vida Parayum Munpe and Padayottam, Prem Nazir moved from portrayals of romance to mythology and social reform. He holds two Guinness World Records for playing the lead in over 700 films and for 130 films opposite Sheela, and received the Padma Bhushan in 1983.
Prem Nazir
Actor Raaj Kumar and Music Director Bombay Ravi in
Waqt
Legendary actor Raaj Kumar, whose distinctive screen presence was defined by his commanding baritone, eloquent dialogue delivery and unmistakable larger-than-life persona, came together with famed music director Ravi in Yash Chopra’s multi-starrer film Waqt. The film is remembered for Raaj Kumar’s captivating portrayal of a thief named Raja and Ravi’s composition of the popular song ‘Ae Meri Zohra Jabeen’.
Raaj Kumar debuted in the film Rangili (1952) and rose through his performances in Nausherwan-e-Adil and Mother India to Dil Ek Mandir (1963). Later on, he delivered iconic roles in Waqt, Heer Ranjhaa, Pakeezah, Tirangaa among others.
Ravi Shankar Sharma, who is popularly known in Malayalam cinema as Bombay Ravi, started his career in hindi cinema with Vachan (1955). He is known for music created for Chaudhvin Ka Chand, Gumrah, Waqt and Humraaz. He won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Parinayam and Sukrutham.
Raaj Kumar                                       Ravi
Through this specially curated
Centenary Tributes
, the 57th IFFI will celebrate not merely seven extraordinary individuals, but also the enduring creative legacy they have left behind. Their legacy continues to inspire generations and illuminate the timeless richness of Indian cinema.
A century after their birth, the works of these seven stalwarts remain a testament to the extraordinary diversity, creative ambition and artistic excellence of Indian cinema. Through these restored classics, the 57th IFFI offers audiences an opportunity to revisit not just memorable performances, melodies and stories, but also the cinematic traditions and cultural histories they helped shape.
More than a tribute to seven individual legacies, this centenary celebration is a reaffirmation of the importance of preserving India's film heritage and keeping it accessible to future generations.

title: Sixth edition of Creative Minds of Tomorrow (CMOT) inaugurated at 57th IFFI
subtitle:
100 Young Creative Talents across India to participate in 48-Hour Filmmaking Challenge under a theme Roots and Wings: Honouring our roots, Embracing our future

Secretary, Ministry of I&B, Shri Chanchal Kumar urges young filmmakers to draw inspiration from their roots and culture
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
The sixth edition of Creative Minds of Tomorrow (CMOT), an initiative of the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting implemented by the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC), was inaugurated today at Kala Academy, Goa, as part of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).
The initiative brings together 100 young creative talents from across India, providing them a platform to collaborate, showcase their skills and gain industry exposure.
The inaugural ceremony was attended by Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, along with Shri Prabhat, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, Shri Loukik Parakh, Registrar, FTII, Shri K. K. Nirala, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, Shri
G. Krishnakumar
, Chairman, NFDC and Shri Gautam Bhanot, General Manager, NFDC.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Chanchal Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, stated that each participant was present because they had already made their mark, and the next 48 hours would provide them an opportunity to turn that talent into a film.
He observed that roots are drawn from culture, language and experiences, while dreams emerge from imagination, curiosity and the courage to try something new. Referring to French philosopher Joseph Joubert, he noted that imagination helps one dream, learning the craft gives those dreams direction, and roots give stories their voice.
He urged the participants to draw inspiration from their origins, without limiting the reach of their stories. A story originating from a small village in India, if narrated with honesty, can resonate with audiences across the world, he added.
He further emphasised that cinema is a collaborative art form and called upon the participants to listen to one another, trust their teammates, experiment, take creative risks and enjoy the process. He concluded by urging them to carry their roots, allow their imagination to fly, and present their stories to the world.
A key highlight of the inaugural ceremony was the formal launch of the 48-Hour Filmmaking Challenge. The Secretary ceremonially clapped the customised film slate, marking the commencement of the sixth edition of the challenge.
The 2026 cohort comprises 100 participants representing 13 filmmaking crafts, including direction, acting, cinematography, editing and subtitling, scriptwriting, playback singing, music composition, sound recording, costume design, hair and makeup, art direction, animation, visual effects (VFX), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and voice-over and dubbing.
Conducted by the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune, in collaboration with NFDC, the 48-Hour Filmmaking Challenge will see participants in 5 teams work together to conceptualise and produce short films within a 48-hour production window. The completed films will be specially screened at IFFI and evaluated by an eminent jury of film industry professionals.
The CMOT Talent Camp will further connect participants with the media and entertainment industry, offering opportunities to interact with production houses, studios, music labels, OTT platforms, broadcasters and other industry stakeholders.
Since its inception in 2021, CMOT has developed into a platform connecting emerging creative professionals with the media and entertainment industry. Its alumni have gone on to work on international productions and have received recognition at platforms and festivals including Cannes, the Berlinale, the Toronto International Film Festival and the International Emmy Awards.
In a notable outcome, 18 participants from the previous edition were selected by Mukesh Chhabra Casting Company (MCCC), marking an encouraging step towards translating the talent nurtured through CMOT into professional opportunities.

title: Films may not change the world overnight, but can open minds and encourage dialogue: Fatherland Producer Ewa Puszczyńska
subtitle: Discussions to continue for film on the shared history between India and Poland: Ewa Puszczyńska
content:
Goa, 21 November 2026
Films may not change the world overnight, but they can open minds, encourage dialogue and inspire people to reflect on the world around them, said acclaimed Polish film producer Ms. Ewa Puszczyńska, producer of
Fatherland
, the opening film of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).
Addressing a press conference at IFFI, she emphasised the role of cinema in bringing people closer by encouraging conversations and fostering an understanding of diverse perspectives. “
We have to talk to people through our films. We have to open people's minds to other sides of life, to other sides of the world
,” she said.
Reflecting on the divisions in contemporary societies, Ms. Puszczyńska observed that no single narrative or agenda could claim to represent the only valid perspective. She noted that people increasingly tend to hold on to their own narratives rather than listen to one another. “
There is no one agenda, no one narration which is right. Talk to each other, let's find the common ground
,” she said.
Describing
Fatherland
as a story with multiple layers, Ms. Puszczyńska highlighted that the film explores themes that resonate with the contemporary world. Set against the backdrop of a divided Europe in 1949, it reflects the East-West divide and the divisions that continue to shape societies today. The film also raises questions about identity and belonging, particularly in a world marked by migration. “Where is your fatherland? Is it the country you live in, or is it the language you speak? Is it where your history comes from, or is it the country where you live?” she asked, explaining how the film examines the complex relationship between individuals and their homeland.
Through the story of celebrated German writer Thomas Mann and his family,
Fatherland
also explores the relationship between culture and society. Ms. Puszczyńska observed that literature and cultural figures can provide people with role models and sources of inspiration. The film further examines complex family relationships, including those between parents and children, siblings and artists. It also explores the challenges faced by children of celebrated artists and the expectations surrounding their ability to match their parents' achievements. At a broader level, the film examines how major historical developments shape the everyday lives of individuals.
Explaining the film's visual treatment, Ms. Puszczyńska said
Fatherland
was shot in black and white and in a 4:3 aspect ratio, following the visual approach adopted in her earlier collaborations with director Paweł Pawlikowski,
Ida
and
Cold War
. The choice was intended to lend authenticity to the period depicted in the film. “
We wanted the film to look authentic for the times we were talking about. Fatherland may be treated as the third film in the trilogy
,” she said.
Speaking about the production process, she explained that
Fatherland
is an international co-production involving Poland, Germany, Italy and France. Although the story is set in Germany, nearly 95 per cent of the film was shot in Poland, with the creative and technical teams comprising largely Polish professionals. Poland offered suitable locations that could recreate the appearance of Germany in 1949, including ruined and neglected streets, buildings and small towns.
Ms. Puszczyńska also expressed interest in exploring a film based on the shared history of India and Poland, particularly the story of Polish children who found refuge in India during the Second World War. Referring to her conversation with IFFI Festival Director Shri Ashutosh Gowariker, who has already written a script on the subject, she expressed hope that discussions could continue and the possibility of taking the project forward could be explored.
The session was moderated by Shri Sayyid Rabeehashmi.

title: Workers’ welfare and industrial growth are twin wheels of the vehicle of national progress, says Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya
subtitle:
Implementation of Labour Codes is a milestone in India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat, highlights Union Minister Dr. Mandaviya

India's workforce has a foundational role in nation-building, states Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel

Two-Day Chintan Shivir of Labour and Employment Ministers of States & UTs Begins in Gandhinagar
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 1:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The two-day Chintan Shivir of Labour and Employment Ministers of States and Union Territories commenced today at Mahatma Mandir, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. Organised by the Ministry of Labour & Employment (MoLE), Government of India, on 21–22 November 2026, the Chintan Shivir marks one year since the coming into effect of the Labour Codes on 21 November 2025.
The inaugural session of the conclave was co-chaired by Shri Bhupendra Patel, Chief Minister of Gujarat and Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Minister of Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, with the participation of Sushri Shobha Karandlaje, Union Minister of State for Labour & Employment and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), alongside Labour, Employment and Industry Ministers and senior officials from States and Union Territories.
Delivering the Opening Address, Union Minister of Labour & Employment,
Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya
, described workers’ welfare and industrial growth as the twin wheels of the vehicle of national progress. Strengthening industries while safeguarding workers’ interests is essential for India’s development and economic growth, he emphasised.
केंद्रीय श्रम एवं रोजगार मंत्री डॉ. मनसुख मांडविया ने आज गांधीनगर, गुजरात में आयोजित दो दिवसीय चिंतन शिविर के उद्घाटन सत्र को संबोधित किया।

उन्होंने कहा कि श्रमिक कल्याण और उद्योगों की प्रगति एक-दूसरे के पूरक हैं। 

#MoLE #ChintanShivir2026 https://t.co/fIx2WSxc3C
— Ministry of Labour & Employment, GoI (@LabourMinistry)
November 21, 2026
Highlighting the implementation of Labour Codes as a significant milestone in India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat, the Union Minister noted that the Codes ensure provisions for minimum wages, expanding social security and fixed-term employment, among others, while reducing compliance burdens on industries and fostering growth. He also drew attention to the remarkable expansion of India’s social security coverage from 25 crore in 2014 to 101 crore in 2026, underlining the Government's commitment to workers’ welfare.
Referring to the rising global demand for India’s skilled workforce and the country’s demographic advantage, he underscored the need for deliberations on international employment opportunities for youth and the mobility of Indian workers across borders.
He called upon all stakeholders to work collectively in the spirit of Team India towards the welfare of the country’s seven crore workers. Invoking the fifth of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s ‘Panch Pran’ urging 140 crore citizens to work collectively towards achieving national goals, he invited participants to engage actively in deliberations at the Chintan Shivir, while also encouraging them to explore Gujarat and witness its rich culture and history.
Shri Bhupendra Patel
, Chief Minister of Gujarat, delivering the Keynote Address, underscored that the dignity, welfare and empowerment of workers are integral to India’s progress and nation-building. Reflecting on the transformative efforts undertaken over the past year in the implementation of Labour Codes, he highlighted the emergence of a stronger, more worker-centric labour ecosystem.
The Chief Minister also emphasised the Chintan Shivir’s role as a platform for States and UTs to exchange best practices, strengthen cooperation and advance a shared vision for labour welfare and industrial growth. Reaffirming the foundational role of the workforce in shaping India’s future, he stressed that Shramik Kalyan and industrial development must go hand in hand as the nation advances towards becoming a global economic powerhouse.
Earlier, delivering the Welcome Address and Introductory Remarks,
Dr. Chandra Bhushan Kumar
, Secretary (Labour & Employment), MoLE, extended a warm welcome to all dignitaries and participants from across the country. He emphasized the need for a change in mindset and perspective for the effective implementation of the Labour Codes, noting that focused deliberations are essential to deliver effectively on the responsibilities and expectations on the journey ahead.
Highlighting that these discussions are vital in helping translate the goal of Viksit Bharat into reality, he called upon all participants to share insights on best practices from their respective States and Union Territories, and uphold their collective responsibility to make the Chintan Shivir a success.
Following the inaugural session, Day 1 (21st November 2026) features four thematic plenary sessions covering Labour Codes – Implementation Status & Way Forward, Employment Initiatives and EPFO Reforms, Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) Reforms, and Social Security for Unorganized Workers & Labour Statistics, alongside State/UT best-practice videos and discussions. Concurrently, parallel Breakaway Sessions for State/UT field officials are being held on implementation strategies for the Labour Codes, MSME engagement, field-level initiatives, and trust-based electronic compliances.

title: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Celebrated Women Entrepreneurship Day on 19th November, 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 1:06PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Government of India, celebrated
Women Entrepreneurship Day 2026 in
association with India SME Forum in New Delhi on 19 November 2026. The event brought together policymakers, industry leaders, financial institutions, development  partners and women entrepreneurs to deliberate on strengthening the ecosystem for women-led enterprises.
The event was organised around four key themes – Enable, Accelerate, Digitise and Globalise– focusing on facilitating the transition of women from aspiring entrepreneurs to successful business leaders with greater access to finance, markets, technology and global value chains. The deliberations aimed to position women entrepreneurs as key drivers of inclusive economic growth and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
The event was graced by Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi, Union Minister of MSME, as the Chief Guest and Sushri Shobha Karandlaje, Minister of State for MSME and Labour & Employment graced the event as the Guest of Honour. The event was also attended by Shri Kalraj Mishra, Former Governor of Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh and Chief Patron, India SME Forum; Shri Bharat Khera, Secretary, Ministry of MSME; along-with Senior Officers of Ministry of MSME, industry representatives, women entrepreneurs and other distinguished dignitaries.
Representatives from various Central Ministries and institutions, including the Ministry of Rural Development, MeitY, Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and SIDBI, participated in the conference. Representatives of State Rural Livelihood Missions from Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Jammu & Kashmir, along with development and philanthropic organisations such as UN Women, Empower, Gates Foundation, Digital Empowerment Foundation and Vedanta's CSR arm, also contributed to the deliberations.
Key Addresses and Highlights
Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi, Union Minister of MSME, highlighted the multifaceted role of women in strengthening families, society and the economy, noting that nearly 38% of MSMEs are women-led. He emphasised the importance of Ministry’s schemes in supporting women entrepreneurs and highlighted international collaborations and amendments to the MSME Development Act, 2026, as key enablers for expanding market opportunities, strengthening the MSME ecosystem and facilitating timely payments through TReDS.
In her keynote address, Sushri Shobha Karandlaje, Minister of State for MSME and Labour & Employment, emphasised that financial independence is essential for empowering women to emerge as leaders in businesses, families and communities. She highlighted the growing financial credibility of women entrepreneurs and noted that the RBI's recognition of women-led Self-Help Groups (SHGs) as reliable borrowers reflects the increasing confidence in their financial capabilities. Highlighting the contribution of various Government initiatives towards women’s economic empowerment, she stated that the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) has supported the generation of over 25 lakh jobs for women, while public procurement from women-owned Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) has exceeded the mandatory 3% procurement target
Also, Shri Kalraj Mishra, Former Governor of Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh and Chief Patron, India SME Forum, stressed the need to transform women from job seekers into job creators to realise the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat. Referring to initiatives such as Lakhpati Didi, he highlighted the importance of connecting grassroots skills and local production capabilities with global value chains through digitalisation, access to growth capital and sustained institutional support.
Shri Bharat Khera, Secretary, Ministry of MSME, highlighted the significant progress in strengthening women's participation in the MSME sector, noting that women-owned enterprises account for approximately 38% of the more than 10 crore enterprises registered with the Ministry. He reiterated the Government's vision to bring gender parity in MSME Ecosystem.
He emphasised the need to move beyond enterprise formalisation towards enabling women-led businesses to become market leaders through enhanced access to global markets, equity investments and integration into diverse value chains.
Further, Dr. Rajneesh, Additional Secretary & Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME, highlighted the vital contribution of women entrepreneurs to India's economic growth, describing them as a key X-factor behind the country's 7.8% economic growth.
He noted that rising female labour force participation, improved access to business credit and emerging opportunities through India's Free Trade Agreements are creating an enabling environment for women to contribute more significantly to enterprise development and nation-building.
Four Thematic Technical Sessions: Enabling, Accelerating, Scaling and Globalising Women-Led Enterprises
The conference featured four technical sessions, bringing together women entrepreneurs, industry experts, policymakers and international representatives to discuss practical pathways for strengthening women-led enterprises.
Session I – ENABLE: From Aspiration to Enterprise
Chaired by Ms. RukmaniAttri, Joint Development Commissioner, Ministry of MSME, the session focused on creating an enabling ecosystem for aspiring women entrepreneurs.
Session II – ACCELERATE: From Survival to Scale
Chaired and moderated by Shri Vinamra Mishra, Joint Secretary, Ministry of MSME, the session explored strategies to help women-led enterprises scale up and become competitive.
Session III – DIGITISE: Empowering Women through Digitalisation
Chaired and moderated by Ms. Ankita Pandey, Director, Ministry of MSME, the session examined the role of digital technologies in expanding opportunities for women entrepreneurs.
Session IV – GLOBALISE: From Local to Global
Chaired and moderated by Ms. Mercy Epao, Joint Secretary (SME), Ministry of MSME, the session focused on enhancing the participation of women-led enterprises in international trade and global value chains.
Reaffirming the Commitment to Women-Led Enterprise Development
Women Entrepreneurship Day 2026 reaffirmed the importance of women's participation in enterprise development, employment generation and inclusive economic growth. The conference provided a platform for dialogue and collaboration among government, industry, financial institutions and development partners to identify actionable pathways for strengthening women-led businesses.
The Ministry of MSME remains committed to fostering an enabling ecosystem that ensures women entrepreneurs have access to finance, technology, skills, markets and global opportunities, empowering them to transform their aspirations into successful enterprises and contribute meaningfully to the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh Hosts Lunch for  Delhi University and JNU students hailing from J&K, mostly Jammu region
subtitle:
Dr. Jitendra Singh Assures Jammu Students in Delhi of Support; Says They Can Reach Out to Him as Their “Local Guardian”

Students Discuss Hostel Concerns, Career Opportunities, Employment Prospects and Issues Related to J&K

Students Appreciate Dr Jitendra Singh's Development Initiatives and Government Schemes in Jammu; Dr. Jitendra Singh Shares Experiences from His Student Days

Minister Encourages Students to Become Good Learners and Strengthen Jammu’s Representation on National and International Platforms
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 5:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh today  hosted a lunch at his residence in New Delhi for Delhi University (DU) and Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) students hailing from Jammu & Kashmir, mostly from Jammu, who are pursuing higher education in various institutions of Delhi.
During the interaction, the Minister assured the students that they could reach out to him directly for any problem, assistance or facilitation required during their stay in Delhi, saying he was like their “local guardian”.
Dr. Jitendra Singh encouraged them to pursue their academic and professional aspirations with confidence and appreciated the growing number of students from Jammu and Kashmir moving to Delhi for higher education in diverse disciplines, including specialised subjects such as European Studies and International Studies.
The interaction brought together students from Delhi University, JNU, Delhi School of Economics, and other academic streams. Many of the students including Sachiv Sharma, Atavika Chandan, Karmang Raina, Saksham Khajuria, Palak Jasrotia, Monalika Sharma, Aditya Jamwal, Migrank Magotra, Abhishek Khajuria, Vanshika Sumbria, Dheeraj Kumar, Shivam Rajput and Aditya Baru participated in the interaction, sharing their experiences, aspirations and concerns.
The students discussed issues concerning hostel accommodation, career opportunities, employment prospects and other matters affecting the youth from J&K. They also raised issues related to Jammu and exchanged views on the region's development and future prospects. Students expressed appreciation for the Government’s efforts, development initiatives and schemes in Jammu, reflecting their positive perspective on the progress being undertaken in the region.
Dr. Jitendra Singh encouraged the students to cultivate the habit of being good learners, remain curious and continuously expand their knowledge beyond formal academic pursuits. Sharing experiences from his own student days, he spoke about the importance of learning, perseverance and staying connected with one's roots while pursuing opportunities in wider academic and professional arenas.
The interaction also included discussion on strengthening the representation of Jammu’s youth on national and international platforms, enabling them to contribute to wider discourse, opportunities and emerging fields.
Accommodation and dining-related concerns raised by the students, including issues concerning hostel facilities and the mess, were immediately taken up by the Minister with the concerned authorities of Delhi University for necessary attention. The students also suggested introducing a few additional dishes in the dining menu of the University mess and canteen, adding a lighter and personal dimension to the interaction.
Reiterating his assurance of support, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the students should not hesitate to contact him whenever they face any difficulty or require any assistance in Delhi. The interaction brought together student welfare, mentorship and an exchange of views on J&K’s development, with the Minister encouraging young people to make the most of their educational opportunities and emerge as confident contributors to the nation.

title: BRIC aims at USD 300 billion Indian bioeconomy by 2030 and USD 1 trillion by 2047: Dr. Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
BRIC’s Integrated Science Model Pioneered a New Approach to Institutional Collaboration in Government; Other Organisations Followed: Dr. Jitendra Singh at BRIC’s 4th AGM

Union Minister calls for accelerating research translation, strengthening industry partnerships and attracting global scientific talent

BRIC’s collaborative research model, shared infrastructure and interdisciplinary programmes to strengthen India’s biotechnology ecosystem, says Dr. Jitendra Singh
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 5:05PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh said today  that BRIC aims at  USD 300 billion Indian bioeconomy by 2030 and a USD 1 trillion bioeconomy by 2047.
The integration of biotechnology research institutions under the Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council (BRIC) was among the first initiatives of its kind in the Government of India, demonstrating a pioneering model of institutional integration that has subsequently inspired similar approaches across other organisations,  said the Minister.
Addressing the Fourth Annual General Meeting of the BRIC Society, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the initiative was conceived to bring institutions together through shared resources, collaborative science and integrated governance, while retaining their scientific strengths. He said India's biotechnology transformation, with the bioeconomy growing from around USD 10 billion to over USD 195 billion, has contributed significantly to the country's development journey, reflecting the expanding role of science, innovation and technology in national growth.
The Fourth Annual General Meeting of the Biotechnology Research and Innovation Council (BRIC) Society was held at Kartavya Bhawan, New Delhi, under the chairmanship of Dr. Jitendra Singh, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and Minister of State in the Prime Minister’s Office, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Government of India, and President, BRIC Society.
The meeting reviewed BRIC’s institutional progress, scientific achievements, governance reforms, research collaborations and future priorities. Dr. Rajesh S. Gokhale, Secretary, Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and Director General, BRIC, made a detailed presentation on the Council’s achievements and activities, followed by deliberations and inputs from Society members, including those participating virtually.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said BRIC represents a new approach to scientific institution-building in India, where institutions work collectively, share capabilities and pursue multidisciplinary research while retaining their individual strengths. He welcomed BRIC’s continued strong research performance, ranking first among government institutions in health sciences and second in biological sciences in India for the second consecutive year, as per the Nature Index India. He said scientific achievements must not remain confined to publications and patents but translate into technologies, products and solutions that make a tangible difference to people’s lives.
The Minister referred to research emerging from BRIC institutions across healthcare, agriculture, animal health, advanced materials and technology platforms, including novel therapeutics, diagnostics, disease detection, climate-resilient agriculture and sustainable biomaterials. He stressed that research priorities must increasingly be aligned with national needs and societal challenges, benefiting patients, farmers, industries and communities.
Dr. Jitendra Singh called for stronger engagement between scientists, entrepreneurs, investors and industry from the early stages of technology development. He said research translation requires capital, mentorship, industry partnerships and a better understanding of market and regulatory pathways, and that the journey from laboratory to market must become a natural extension of the research ecosystem.
The Minister welcomed initiatives such as the Entrepreneur-in-Residence programme and collaborations aimed at strengthening biomanufacturing, technology scale-up and commercialisation. He encouraged BRIC institutions to build deeper connections with industry and innovation networks, enabling researchers to take their discoveries forward into startups, products and commercially viable technologies.
Dr. Jitendra Singh emphasised the importance of creating an enabling ecosystem for young scientists and innovators, encouraging them to move beyond publications and patents towards product development, technology translation and enterprise creation. He said India’s expanding biotechnology startup ecosystem, now comprising more than 11,000 startups, reflects growing confidence in the country’s scientific and entrepreneurial capabilities.
During the deliberations, Society members participating virtually also emphasised opportunities in AI and biology, technology development and attracting Indian scientific talent working abroad to return and contribute to the country’s research ecosystem. Suggestions included leveraging platforms such as Vaibhav Connect to connect the scientific diaspora with research opportunities in BRIC institutions, strengthening interdisciplinary engagement with social sciences to address societal challenges, and expanding collaboration with entrepreneurs and industry to accelerate innovation.
Referring to the D.E.S.I.G.N. for BioE3 Challenge, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the initiative has mobilised young people across the country towards biotechnology innovation, with more than 6,000 proposals received from school students and citizens across both categories. He encouraged BRIC to continue nurturing talent, attracting promising researchers and creating opportunities for ambitious interdisciplinary research. He also stressed the importance of communicating scientific research in accessible formats so that its relevance and societal benefits reach a wider audience.
Dr. Jitendra Singh welcomed the strengthening of BRIC’s governance and institutional framework, including the operationalisation of its Secretariat and efforts to reinforce research capacity through recruitment against revived scientific positions. He said institutional integration, shared infrastructure and collaborative research must continue to create new opportunities for scientific talent and strengthen India’s research capabilities.
The AGM also witnessed the launch of the BRIC Handbook of Memorandum of Association (MoA), Rules, Regulations and Bye-laws by Dr. Jitendra Singh, providing a consolidated reference for the governance and functioning of the Council. Members were also apprised of strategic initiatives, governance activities and the proposal concerning the dissolution of existing societies of constituent autonomous institutions and their merger with BRIC as part of the ongoing institutional restructuring.
Emphasising the road ahead, the Minister said India’s ambition of building a USD 300 billion bioeconomy by 2030 and a USD 1 trillion bioeconomy by 2047 calls for greater scale in scientific innovation, research translation, industry participation and talent development. He called upon BRIC to continue emerging as a globally recognised platform for collaborative science, breakthrough innovation and technology-led national development, ensuring that the benefits of biotechnology reach farmers, patients, industries and communities across the country.

title: CSIR-NEERI brings experts together to find solutions to air pollution
subtitle: Experts from MoEF and CC, DST, DBT and CSIR Institutes discuss scientific solutions, technologies and coordinated action for cleaner air
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 4:45PM by PIB Delhi
content:
CSIR–National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) organised a Brainstorming Workshop on “Clean Air and Climate Resilience for the Indo-Gangetic Plains (IGP-CACR)” at its Delhi Regional Centre, Naraina, New Delhi.
The workshop brought together scientists, policymakers and technical experts to identify practical, science-based solutions to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and the wider Indo-Gangetic Plains. Discussions covered airshed management, pollution sources, health impacts, climate vulnerability, pollution-control technologies, artificial intelligence-based decision-support systems and institutional partnerships. The focus was on solutions that can be implemented on a large scale and deliver measurable improvements in air quality.
The workshop was held under the leadership of Dr. S. Venkata Mohan, Director, CSIR-NEERI. It was attended by Dr. G. V. Raghunath Reddy, Scientist-F, Department of Science and Technology (DST); Dr. N. Subrahmanyam, Scientist-E, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC); and Dr. Balendra Singh, Scientist-D, Department of Biotechnology (DBT). Senior representatives from CSIR Headquarters included Dr. Shailaja Donempudi, Distinguished Scientist and Head, BDG and Dr. Anirban Pal, Scientist-G and Head, CPD.
Participants from various ministries and CSIR institutions during the Brainstorming Workshop on “Clean Air and Climate Resilience for the Indo-Gangetic Plains” at CSIR-NEERI Delhi Regional Centre, New Delhi.
Dr. S. K. Goyal, Scientist-G and Chair, CSIR-NEERI Delhi Regional Centre, highlighted the major air pollution challenges in Delhi-NCR and Indo-Gangetic Plains. He stressed the need for coordinated airshed management, stronger air quality monitoring networks and an integrated PAN-CSIR mission to convert scientific findings into practical solutions and policy measures.
During the discussions, Dr. N. Subrahmanyam (MoEF&CC) emphasised the need to set up a technical committee for the Indo-Gangetic Plains to identify priority areas for action and develop a scientific approach for planning India's Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring (CAAQM) network. Dr. Balendra Singh (DBT) highlighted emerging research opportunities in precision nutrition and human microbiome, particularly their links with health effects caused by air pollution. Dr. G. V. Raghunath Reddy (DST) suggested that CSIR prepare a structured list of potential interventions, identifying suitable locations and scales for their implementation to support demonstration projects.
Dr. Shailaja Donempudi, CSIR Headquarters, stressed the need to make greater use of CSIR technologies, particularly those that have reached Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 and above, through field demonstrations and wider deployment across the Indo-Gangetic Plains. Dr. Anirban Pal, CSIR Headquarters, highlighted the importance of developing technologies for specific pollution sources, along with clear implementation plans, defined institutional responsibilities and measurable outcomes.
CSIR experts deliberating during the Brainstorming Workshop on “Clean Air and Climate Resilience for the Indo-Gangetic Plains”, organised by CSIR-NEERI at its Delhi Regional Centre, New Delhi
Scientists and experts from CSIR-NEERI's four Regional Centres at Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Hyderabad and other CSIR laboratories and units actively participated in the workshop. These included CSIR-IIP, CSIR-CDRI, CSIR-IHBT, CSIR-IMTECH, CSIR-CRRI, CSIR-CBRI, CSIR-CMERI, CSIR-NIScPR and CSIR-NIDSA, along with CSIR's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) and Technology Management Directorate. The technical sessions were coordinated by Dr. Ankit Gupta, Scientist-E and Dr. Sunil Gulia, Scientist-D, CSIR-NEERI Delhi Regional Centre.
Highlighting the way forward, Dr. S. Venkata Mohan, Director, CSIR-NEERI stated that the institute would bring together the scientific and institutional recommendations from the workshop into a policy-level brief. The brief will identify priority interventions, technology readiness, potential demonstration projects and opportunities for collaboration. It will help support science-based decisions and coordinated action to improve air quality and strengthen climate resilience across Delhi-NCR and Indo-Gangetic Plains.
The workshop highlighted the need for a coordinated, science-based and action-oriented approach, moving beyond isolated measures to address recurring air pollution challenges and build climate resilience across the region.

title: NISD Exchanges 23 MoUs with Universities and Institutions Across India to Strengthen Social Defence Initiatives
subtitle:
Institutional Partnerships Expand to 30, Promoting Prevention Education, Research, Training and Capacity Building Across Social Defence Areas

MoUs to Strengthen Collaborative Efforts for Drug Abuse Prevention, Welfare of Senior Citizens, Transgender Welfare and Prevention of Beggary
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 8:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Institute of Social Defence (NISD), under Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India, organised an MoU Exchange Ceremony at its campus in the National Capital, here today.
The ceremony was graced by Dr Virendra Kumar, Hon’ble Union Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, Shri Sudhansh Pant, Union Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, Dr Sandeep Rewaji Rathod, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice And Empowerment and Shri Gaurav Singh Rajawat, Director, NISD, New Delhi, and other senior officers of the Ministry.
On the occasion, 23 Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) were exchanged between NISD and universities and institutions from across the country.
Out of these, 15 institutions participated in person and 8 institutions joined virtually. With this, NISD’s institutional partnerships have increased to 30, building upon the 7 MoUs signed earlier with universities and organisations.
Addressing the gathering, Union Minister Dr. Virendra Kumar said the exchange of MoUs with 23 institutions across the country marks a significant and historic initiative towards strengthening the work of NISD through institutional collaboration.
He emphasised that partnerships with universities, rural development institutes and other reputed institutions can help advance training, capacity building, rehabilitation, livelihood opportunities and social inclusion for individuals affected by substance use, transgender persons, senior citizens and persons vulnerable to beggary.
The Minister said the initiative would strengthen efforts towards enabling vulnerable individuals to lead dignified, self-reliant lives and contribute meaningfully to society.
Dr Kumar underscored the need to have regular dialogue and consultations, review of initiatives and sharing of best practices among institutions would help extend effective interventions across different States and regions.
Shri Sudhansh Pant, Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, highlighted the important role of educational institutions in preventing drug abuse among young people. He enjoined upon institutions to organise regular anti-drug awareness activities and pledges, enabling students to carry the message of drug prevention from their campuses to families, peers and communities. Shri Pant also stressed the need for regular coordination, monitoring and mutually beneficial training programmes between NISD and partner institutions.
The Secretary said that sustained awareness activities, including periodic anti-drug pledges in educational institutions, could help create a wider chain of awareness and collective action towards a drug-free India. He urged NISD and its partner institutions to explore regular coordination, monitoring and short-term training programmes within campuses to strengthen collaborative efforts in drug abuse prevention.
The 23 institutions include State Institute of Rural Development, Ranchi, Jharkhand; State Institute of Rural Development, Meghalaya; State Institute of Rural Development (SIRD), Manipur; Telangana Institute of Rural Development (TGIRD), Telangana; Central University of Andhra Pradesh; Central University of Karnataka; Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar University, Lucknow; National Law University, Jodhpur; Shri Vishwakarma Skill University, Haryana; and Dr. Manmohan Singh Bengaluru City University,
Karnataka.
In addition, CHRIST University, Bengaluru; Yenepoya (Deemed to be University), Karnataka; Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi; Aligarh Muslim University, Uttar Pradesh; Indian Adult Education Association, New Delhi; Andhra Pradesh State Institute of Panchayat Raj & Rural Development; AIIMS Jodhpur, Rajasthan; Administrative Training Centre, Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA), Puducherry; Kerala Institute of Local Administration (KILA), Kerala; Maharashtra National Law University, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar; Chanakya National Law University, Patna; Mahatma Gandhi Central University, Bihar; and Maharashtra National Law University, Nagpur, are among other institutions who signed MoUs with NISD.
The scope of these MoUs covers Prevention Education, Research, Training and Capacity Building, Curriculum Development, and Outreach and Advocacy in the field of Social Defence, including Drug Abuse Prevention, Welfare of Senior Citizens, Transgender Welfare and Prevention of Beggary.
The partnerships are expected to facilitate institutional collaboration, knowledge exchange, training opportunities and the development of effective interventions across these areas.
The Union Minister administered
‘Senior Citizen’
and
‘Anti Drug’
Pledges to the participants, refreshing the sense of responsibility towards working for creating awareness among common masses, to uphold respect,  dignity and and to ensure healthcare and welfare of the senior citizens besides Drug Abuse Prevention and treatment and rehabilitation of the persons affected by the substance abuse.
The expanded network of institutional partnerships is expected to create a sustained framework for training, awareness generation, research and evidence-based interventions in the field of Social Defence.
Through collaboration with universities, public training institutions and specialised organisations across the country, NISD will further strengthen its efforts towards the welfare, rehabilitation, empowerment and social inclusion of vulnerable sections of society.
The initiative reinforces the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment’s commitment to strengthening institutional collaboration and advancing a socially secure, inclusive and empowered India.

title: India’s Expanding Regional Exports
subtitle: Africa and Asia lead growth across global markets
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 NOV 2026 12:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s merchandise exports recorded broad-based growth across major global regions during April-September 2026-27.
Exports to Africa
registered the
highest growth of 44%
, followed by Asia at 21%. The Americas recorded 13% growth, while Europe and CIS & Baltics registered increases of 8% and 7%, respectively. Engineering goods, electronic goods and petroleum products remained important export categories. Strong performance across diverse markets and product groups reflects the expanding reach of India’s merchandise exports across global regions.
India’s Exports Strengthen Across Global Regions
India’s exports recorded broad-based growth across major global regions during
April–September 2026-27
, with
Africa and Asia emerging as the fastest-growing regions
.
Exports to Asia increased 21%
from US$ 85.84 billion to US$ 103.84 billion, while exports to Africa surged 44% from US$ 21.87 billion to US$ 31.42 billion. The Americas registered 13% growth to US$ 66.82 billion, followed by Europe at 8% to US$ 51.04 billion and CIS & Baltics at 7% to US$ 3.36 billion.
The regional expansion was supported by demand across a diverse range of markets and export categories. Engineering goods, electronic goods, petroleum products, and chemicals featured prominently across regional export baskets.
Regional Export Performance
Asia: Exports Cross US$ 100 Billion, Led by China and Singapore
India’s exports to Asia increased 21%, from US$ 85.84 billion to US$ 103.84 billion.
Among the major export destinations:
China and Singapore
were the largest markets, with exports reaching US$ 11.39 billion and US$ 11.07 billion, respectively.
Exports to China increased 36%
, while those to
Singapore more than doubled, registering 103% growth
.
Malaysia and Hong Kong
also emerged as significant markets, with exports reaching US$ 5.58 billion and US$ 5.12 billion, respectively.
Malaysia registered 83% growth
, while
Hong Kong recorded 37% growth
.
Other markets
included Bangladesh at US$ 5.66 billion, Nepal at US$ 4.37 billion, Japan and Australia at around US$ 4.10 billion each, Sri Lanka at US$ 3.94 billion, South Korea at US$ 3.91 billion, Vietnam at US$ 3.83 billion and Oman at US$ 3.29 billion.
At the commodity level,
engineering goods
remained the
largest growing category
at US$ 27.47 billion, registering 22% growth. This was followed by petroleum products at US$ 17.05 billion, up 28%.
Electronic goods nearly doubled
to US$ 10.54 billion, growing 91%, while
gems and jewellery
reached
US$ 9.59 billion
and
organic and inorganic chemicals
increased to US$ 6.17 billion
.
Americas: Exports Reach US$ 66.82 Billion, Driven by the US and High-Value Manufacturing
India’s exports to the Americas increased 13%,
from US$ 59.30 billion to US$ 66.82 billion.
Among the major export destinations:
United States:
Accounted for US$ 50.80 billion,
registering 11% growth
and remaining the
largest market in the region
.
Brazil, Mexico and Canada:
Exports reached US$ 4.33 billion, US$ 3.45 billion and US$ 2.67 billion, respectively.
Brazil
registered
14% growth
,
Mexico 26%
and
Canada 18%
.
Other markets:
Colombia and Chile also recorded positive growth.
The region’s growth was anchored by
engineering goods at US$ 19.19 billion, up 21%,
and
electronic goods at US$ 15.35 billion, up 23%. Drugs and pharmaceuticals reached US$ 6.59 billion
, followed by organic and inorganic chemicals at US$ 4.17 billion, gems and jewellery at US$ 3.35 billion and petroleum products at US$ 3.16 billion.
Europe: Exports Reach US$ 51 Billion, with Engineering and Electronics Leading
India’s exports to Europe grew 8%, from US$ 47.06 billion to US$ 51.04 billion.
Among the major export destinations:
United Kingdom and Germany:
The
UK was the largest market
at US$ 7.32 billion, followed by Germany at US$ 6.34 billion, with exports to
Germany increasing 12%.
Spain and Italy:
Exports to
Spain rose 45%
to US$ 4.68 billion, while
Italy recorded 25%
growth to US$ 4.55 billion.
France and Turkey:
Exports to France reached US$ 3.73 billion, while those to Turkey increased 72% to US$ 3.63 billion.
Engineering goods remained the largest growing
commodity category at US$ 15.88 billion, up 12%.
Electronic goods rose 52%
to US$ 5.44 billion, while organic and inorganic chemicals increased to US$ 4.06 billion and drugs and pharmaceuticals to US$ 3.29 billion. Gems and jewellery also grew 19% to US$ 2.20 billion.
Africa: Exports Surge to US$ 31.42 Billion, Led by Petroleum and Engineering Goods
India’s exports to Africa increased strongly by 44%, from US$ 21.87 billion to US$ 31.42 billion.
Among the major export destinations:
South Africa:
Remained the largest market at US$ 5.69 billion,
registering 52% growth
.
Tanzania and Kenya:
Exports reached US$ 4.77 billion and US$ 3.63 billion, respectively.
Tanzania recorded 121% growth
, while exports to
Kenya more than doubled
,
increasing 101%
.
Egypt:
Exports increased 73% to US$ 3.25 billion.
Nigeria and Mozambique:
Also recorded positive growth, reaching US$ 1.78 billion and US$ 1.31 billion, respectively.
At the commodity level,
petroleum products were the largest contributor
at US$ 11.85 billion,
more than doubling with growth of 137%. Engineering goods
reached US$ 7.48 billion,
up 29%,
while drugs and pharmaceuticals stood at US$ 2.58 billion. Organic and inorganic chemicals increased to US$ 1.41 billion, while plastic and linoleum
and meat, dairy and poultry products also recorded strong positive growth.
CIS & Baltics: Exports Rise to US$ 3.36 Billion
India’s exports to the CIS & Baltics increased 7% from US$ 3.14 billion to US$ 3.36 billion.
Among the major export destinations:
Russia:
Remained the
largest growing market
, with
exports rising 7%
to US$ 2.39 billion.
Georgia:
Exports reached US$ 0.25 billion.
Armenia and Kazakhstan:
Also recorded positive growth.
Among growing commodity categories,
organic and inorganic chemicals
reached US$ 0.37 billion,
up 33%.
This was
followed by
meat, dairy and poultry products
at US$ 0.36 billion,
up 36%
, and electronic goods at US$ 0.24 billion. Mica, coal and other ores and minerals reached US$ 0.17 billion, while marine products increased to US$ 0.14 billion.
Diversification Across Markets and Products
The regional trends underline the scale as well as growing diversification of India’s global exports.
Asia
remained the backbone of the
export footprint at over US$ 103 billion
. This was complemented by the US$ 66.82 billion Americas market and US$ 51.04 billion European market. Africa delivered particularly strong expansion to cross US$ 31 billion.
Importantly, growth was supported by large and commercially significant markets such as the United States, China, Singapore, the UK, Germany and South Africa, alongside strong expansion in Malaysia, Spain, Italy, Tanzania and Kenya.
At the product level,
engineering goods
,
electronics
and
petroleum products
accounted for some of the largest growing export values, pointing to a geographically and product-wise diversified expansion in India’s global merchandise exports.
